oidc_jwt.description: Dex does not issue refresh tokens for connectors that do not support offline_access, notably SAML and authproxy; SAML ignores offline_access.
oidc_jwt.note: Missing refresh_token is by design and should not be treated as token freshness enforcement failure.

oidc_jwt.description: Authorization code flow requests without nonce may succeed.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not treat lack of mandatory nonce in pure code flow as a vulnerability by itself.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex rotates refresh tokens on every refresh by default.
oidc_jwt.note: A new refresh token value after refresh is expected and should not be treated as session confusion.

oidc_jwt.description: Dex can intentionally issue an ID token for a different client audience when the target client explicitly lists the acting client in trustedPeers and the request includes the audience:server:client_id:(client-id) scope.
oidc_jwt.note: Cross-client audience changes are by design under explicit trust and should not be flagged as audience confusion.

oidc_jwt.description: Token exchange responses always place the issued token in access_token, regardless of requested_token_type; the actual type is indicated by issued_token_type.
oidc_jwt.note: Parsers must inspect issued_token_type instead of expecting a separate id_token field.

oidc_jwt.description: Claims returned in ID token/UserInfo depend on requested scopes and connector capabilities; groups and preferred_username may be absent unless requested and supported.
oidc_jwt.note: Missing optional claims should not be mistaken for identity corruption or authorization stripping bugs.

oidc_jwt.description: When getUserInfo is enabled on an OIDC connector, claims from the UserInfo endpoint take priority over claims in the ID token.
oidc_jwt.note: Claim differences are expected under this configuration.

oidc_jwt.description: OIDC connector groups claims only refresh when the ID token is refreshed; regular refresh flow does not update groups, and groups are disabled by default unless insecureEnableGroups is set.
oidc_jwt.note: Do not interpret stale groups in an existing session as immediate config-change incoherence.

oidc_jwt.constraint: Dex documentation describes dynamic management through the gRPC API, not documented REST admin endpoints, for clients/connectors/users. Do NOT invent REST setup operations such as enable_auth_method, configure_jwt_validation, create_application, modify_role_config, revoke_session, or cleanup_auth_method from general Dex knowledge; for this protocol run only the documented OIDC/OAuth HTTP endpoints are available.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex as an OIDC provider, include a CONTROL flow using a valid token/code path in the same environment. A failed attack login at /token can also result from bad client credentials, bad code, or unsupported grant configuration rather than time validation alone.

Dex discovery shows authorization_endpoint=/auth and token_endpoint=/token. The fuzzer SHOULD use discovery-derived endpoints and MUST send token and token-exchange requests as application/x-www-form-urlencoded to /token.

Password grant works only when oauth2.passwordConnector is configured and the password grant is enabled. Do NOT treat /token grant_type=password failures as security rejections unless passwordConnector is known to be configured.

Token exchange works only with the OIDC connector and requires connector_id in the /token request. If connector_id is omitted or the upstream connector is not OIDC-capable, failures are expected and are not evidence of issuer/audience enforcement.

For token exchange from upstream access tokens, the OIDC connector must have getUserInfo=true if the upstream access token is opaque. Otherwise Dex may be unable to validate or extract claims from the subject_token, causing false negatives unrelated to the tested invariant.

Dex-issued tokens are client-bound. For I5 audience and cross-client tests, always control client_id and requested scopes explicitly. Cross-client issuance is only expected when the target client explicitly trusts the acting client via trustedPeers and the request uses scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id). Without trustedPeers, cross-client audience requests should fail by design.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, Dex token exchange examples request scope explicitly and Dex supports scopes openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, and audience:server:client_id:(client-id). The fuzzer MUST compare exchanged-token claims against the requested scope set and upstream connector capabilities; missing claims may be due to connector limitations, while extra claims beyond requested scope indicate a binding issue.

For I1/I5 cross-provider JWT audience tests against Dex as relying party for upstream OIDC, configure separate OIDC connectors with distinct clientIDs. Dex documentation states the connector issuer must match discovery and token exchange verifies the submitted subject token against the connector issuer. The fuzzer MUST vary both issuer and client binding per connector; acceptance of a token under the wrong connector would be meaningful only when connectors are distinct.

OIDC connector issuer matching is strict: config.issuer MUST match the issuer returned by upstream discovery unless issuerAlias is explicitly used for off-spec providers. For I1 trust-anchor-substitution and issuer-validation tests, do not misconfigure issuer/issuerAlias in baseline setup or all failures become ambiguous setup errors.

When testing OIDC upstream id_token validation behaviors, Dex documentation references standard OIDC flows and certification. The fuzzer SHOULD test nonce, aud, iss, and exp handling separately, but MUST remember that nonce is primarily relevant to the authorization-code browser flow started at /auth, not RFC 8693 token exchange of an already obtained upstream token.

Dex certification results note oidcc-ensure-request-without-nonce-succeeds-for-code-flow PASSED. For code flow tests, absence of nonce in the authorization request may be accepted by design; do NOT flag missing nonce requirement in pure authorization-code flow as an I2 vulnerability unless the tested scenario specifically requires nonce-bound ID token replay protection.

Dex certification results show oidcc-unsigned-request-object-supported-correctly-or-rejected-as-unsupported as UNKNOWN. For oidc_request_object_alg_none tests, treat both explicit rejection and unsupported behavior as acceptable outcomes; only successful processing of attacker-controlled unsigned request objects should be considered suspicious.

Dex certification results show oidcc-codereuse PASSED and oidcc-codereuse-30seconds WARNING. For I2/I3 code replay tests, use the exact same authorization code twice against /token and judge by HTTP status, not identity differences. A reused code should be rejected; timing-related warnings in certification mean borderline behavior may exist, so keep replay attempts immediate and controlled.

Refresh token rotation is enabled by default: every refresh issues a new refresh token. For any sequence that refreshes tokens, the fuzzer MUST replace the stored refresh token with the newest one after each successful refresh. Reusing an old refresh token after rotation is expected to fail and is not a replay defense bypass.

Refresh token settings have sentinel-like security semantics. disableRotation=true disables per-use refresh token rotation; reuseInterval allows the same previous refresh token to be accepted within a configured interval; validIfNotUsedFor and absoluteLifetime bound refresh token lifetime. Never assume rotation is always active or that replay of the immediately previous refresh token is always rejected when reuseInterval is configured.

offline_access is connector-dependent. Some connectors, notably SAML and authproxy, do not support refresh tokens and SAML ignores offline_access. Do NOT interpret absence of refresh_token in token responses as a security bug unless the chosen connector supports refresh tokens.

Dex documentation for OIDC code flow requires the client to generate and verify the state parameter. For I3 flow-coherence tests such as state_swap, the fuzzer MUST bind each authorization request to a unique state and verify the same state value on callback. A mismatched or reused state is a client-side flow failure, not evidence of a Dex identity mix-up.

Dex documentation and certification results indicate that nonce is not required for pure authorization code flow (oidcc-ensure-request-without-nonce-succeeds-for-code-flow passed). Do NOT flag missing nonce on code-flow authorization requests as an I2 vulnerability. Nonce-based replay checks are relevant to implicit/hybrid ID-token delivery, not standard code flow.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests against Dex-issued tokens, the fuzzer MUST include a control token request using a valid baseline flow. Dex token freshness is governed by configured expiry values, and a failed attack request without a successful control cannot distinguish correct rejection from broken client credentials, bad redirect_uri, or disabled grant type.

Dex token exchange only works with the OIDC connector. For token_exchange tests, the fuzzer MUST configure an upstream connector of type oidc and MUST supply connector_id in the /token request. Omitting connector_id or using a non-OIDC connector causes setup failure rather than a security rejection.

For token_exchange tests using upstream access tokens, Dex documentation states getUserInfo is required if exchanging access tokens to Dex-issued tokens. The fuzzer MUST enable getUserInfo on the OIDC connector when subject_token_type is access_token; otherwise failures are by-design because Dex treats access tokens as opaque.

Dex token exchange requires client authentication via HTTP Basic auth even when the client is marked public for this use case. The fuzzer MUST send client_id/client_secret as Basic credentials on /token for token_exchange tests; missing Basic auth is a request-construction error, not an authorization-binding result.

For I5 token_exchange_scope_escalation tests, Dex issues the exchanged token in the access_token field regardless of requested_token_type, with the actual type indicated by issued_token_type. The fuzzer MUST inspect access_token plus issued_token_type and MUST NOT assume a separate id_token field will be returned.

Dex supports cross-client trust via the dynamic scope audience:server:client_id:(client-id) and trustedPeers on the target client. For audience-binding tests, the fuzzer MUST distinguish by-design delegated audience issuance from unintended audience confusion: if trustedPeers authorizes the requesting client, aud may legitimately differ from the authenticating client and azp will identify the requester.

For I5 cross-client audience tests, the fuzzer MUST configure or omit trustedPeers intentionally. If trustedPeers is present on the target client, requesting scope audience:server:client_id:<target> is by design and should not be flagged as audience escalation. To test missing authorization binding, use a target client that does NOT trust the requesting client.

Dex OIDC connector issuer matching is exact: config.issuer MUST match the issuer returned by upstream discovery, unless issuerAlias is explicitly used to override off-spec providers. For I1 trust-anchor-substitution and issuer-validation tests, the fuzzer MUST set issuer/bound upstream issuer intentionally; otherwise acceptance or rejection may reflect discovery mismatch handling rather than token validation behavior.

Dex OIDC connector allowedGroups is list-membership, not wildcard or regex matching. For I4 multi-identity scenarios, if multiple different users must authenticate through the same connector, the fuzzer MUST either omit allowedGroups or ensure every test identity is actually in at least one configured allowed group. Do NOT set allowedGroups='*' expecting wildcard behavior.

Dex OIDC connector userIDKey and userNameKey are exact claim-name selectors, not pattern matchers. They choose which upstream claim becomes the Dex user identifier/display fields. For I4 collision tests, the fuzzer MUST vary the underlying selected claim value itself; wildcards or regex-like values in these config fields have no matching semantics.

Dex OIDC connector claimMapping fields are exact source-claim name mappings, and overrideClaimMapping=false means standard claims returned in the ID token take precedence over configured mappings. For tests that depend on a nonstandard claim becoming email/preferred_username/groups, the fuzzer MUST set overrideClaimMapping=true when the standard claim is also present; otherwise the mapping will be ignored by design.

Dex OIDC connector claimModifications.filterGroupClaims uses RE2 regex semantics, while allowedGroups uses exact list-membership. For I5 group-policy tests, the fuzzer MUST not confuse these mechanisms: regex filtering can transform the emitted groups set, but authentication gating by allowedGroups still requires exact membership in one configured group.

Dex OIDC connector claimModifications.newGroupFromClaims only supports string claims; non-string claims are skipped. For I5 numeric or boolean claim coercion tests, the fuzzer MUST NOT rely on newGroupFromClaims to surface non-string values into groups. Numeric claims will be skipped rather than coerced.

Dex OIDC connector groups claims may be stale across refresh because groups only refresh when the ID token is refreshed, and insecureEnableGroups is disabled by default. For I3 config-change or I5 group-change tests, the fuzzer MUST use a fresh login or token refresh path as appropriate and MUST NOT expect ordinary session continuity to reflect upstream group changes immediately.

Dex documentation states UserInfo claims take priority over ID token claims when getUserInfo=true. For I4/I5 tests involving conflicting upstream claims, the fuzzer MUST account for this precedence: a mismatch between ID token and UserInfo is resolved in favor of UserInfo by design, not evidence that Dex ignored the ID token inconsistently.

Dex supports unsigned request objects either correctly or by rejecting them as unsupported per certification status, which is listed as unknown/interrupted. For oidc_request_object_alg_none tests, the oracle MUST treat either explicit rejection or unsupported behavior as non-vulnerable unless Dex actually accepts the unsigned request object and applies attacker-controlled parameters.

Dex certification results show PKCE with a valid verifier succeeds, but the docs do not claim PKCE is mandatory for all clients. For pkce_skip and pkce_not_required_public_client checks, assert only that the code exchange without the required verifier is rejected when a code_challenge was used; do NOT compare identities across sessions.

Dex authorization code lifetime is controlled by expiry.authRequests. For I2/I3 code replay and delayed exchange tests, the fuzzer MUST keep exchanges within the configured authRequests window unless intentionally testing expiry, and MUST use a control exchange before concluding a rejection is due to replay protection.

Dex refresh token behavior has security-sensitive sentinels: refreshTokens.disableRotation=true disables per-use rotation, while reuseInterval allows the same previous refresh token to be accepted within a configured interval. Never assume reuseInterval or disableRotation means replay protection is absent globally; they specifically relax refresh-token rotation semantics and can cause apparent replay acceptance by design.

Dex duration fields use explicit duration strings (for example 10m, 6h). The documentation does not define numeric 0 as a universal disable/default sentinel for token expiry settings. The fuzzer MUST NOT assume 0 or empty means disabled for expiry.idTokens, expiry.authRequests, signingKeys, or refresh token lifetimes unless the specific field is documented elsewhere.

Dex does not document a REST admin API for enabling auth methods, configuring JWT validation, creating roles, policies, users, applications, or providers. Test setup for oidc_jwt must be performed via static config file or gRPC API, not inferred REST endpoints.

For I1 trust-anchor-substitution and issuer-validation tests against Dex token exchange, configure the OIDC connector with config.issuer. The submitted subject token is verified against that issuer; without a configured issuer, the intended issuer-binding test is not meaningful.

For I1 cross-provider-jwt-audience and oidc_sso_audience_cross_tenant tests, create two distinct OIDC connectors with different clientIDs. Dex documentation states the connector's clientID/clientSecret identify the upstream RP registration; the fuzzer must present a token minted for connector A to connector B via connector_id and expect rejection.

For I1/I5 audience-binding tests on Dex-issued ID tokens, use the audience:server:client_id:(client-id) scope only when the target client explicitly trusts the requesting client via trustedPeers. Otherwise a changed aud/azp result is invalid test setup rather than a vulnerability.

For I2 expired_token and future_token tests on token_exchange, include a control exchange using a valid upstream token in the same connector configuration. Without a control, exchange failure may be caused by connector misconfiguration, missing client auth, or unsupported token type rather than time-claim enforcement.

For I2 replay_same_token against generic JWT bearer tokens, do NOT treat successful reuse as a vulnerability by default. Dex documentation describes token exchange as exchanging an already-obtained upstream access or ID token and does not document jti tracking or one-time-use semantics for upstream JWTs.

For I3 config-change sequences, Dex configuration is file-based/static in the provided docs. A valid coherence test must restart or reload Dex with the changed connector/client configuration before the second request; merely changing local test assumptions without reconfiguring Dex is invalid.

For I3 authorization-code flow tests, bind the sequence by state and verify the callback uses the same state value returned from the authorization request. Dex documentation explicitly relies on state to link the user who started the flow to the one who finished it and to prevent replay.

For OIDC code-flow tests involving request objects, Dex certification results show 'unsigned request object supported correctly or rejected as unsupported' as an open/unknown area. The fuzzer must treat either explicit rejection or standards-compliant handling as acceptable; only silent acceptance of attacker-controlled parameters with security impact should be flagged.

For PKCE-related OIDC tests, Dex certification results show valid PKCE succeeds, but the docs do not define all failure semantics. Assert non-200/error behavior for malformed or missing verifier cases rather than comparing granted identities.
For token_exchange, send client credentials via HTTP Basic Authentication as documented. Missing or altered client authentication can cause false negatives unrelated to subject_token validation.

For token_exchange using upstream access tokens, set the OIDC connector option getUserInfo=true when the upstream token is an access token and claims must be resolved through UserInfo. Without getUserInfo, access-token exchange may fail or lack claims for reasons unrelated to the invariant under test.

For I4 identity-binding tests on token_exchange, configure the OIDC connector userNameKey/userIDKey deliberately. Dex maps identity from configured upstream claims; changing these mappings changes which upstream field becomes the downstream identity, so collision tests must hold mapping constant across compared logins.

For I4 case/unicode/normalization tests, Dex documentation does not specify normalization or case-folding of subject-like claims. The fuzzer should test raw distinct values as separate identities and only conclude a collision if Dex grants the same downstream identity under identical connector mapping.

For I5 scope-escalation tests on token_exchange, request only scopes documented by Dex (openid, email, profile, groups, federated:id, offline_access, audience:server:client_id:...). Claims absent because the scope was never requested are not evidence of secure filtering, and claims present outside requested scope are the relevant escalation signal.

For I5 token-exchange scope escalation, compare exchanged-token claims against the original requested scope set. Dex docs state scopes control inclusion of claims such as groups and federated_claims; requesting expanded scope during exchange is the correct way to test whether Dex exceeds upstream intent.

For I5 audience tests on Dex-issued tokens, remember Dex binds issued tokens to clients. When testing wrong-audience acceptance, vary the client_id / trustedPeers / audience:server:client_id scope combination explicitly; otherwise audience changes may be by-design cross-client trust rather than a bug.

Token lifetime and rotation settings are duration strings, not numeric sentinels. The docs specify explicit durations like 10m, 6h and do not document 0 or -1 as disable/default sentinels for expiry.idTokens, expiry.authRequests, expiry.deviceRequests, expiry.signingKeys, refreshTokens.validIfNotUsedFor, refreshTokens.absoluteLifetime, or refreshTokens.reuseInterval. Never assume 0 or -1 has special meaning unless verified in implementation.
